title: Globalization
objective: After this level you can explain how supply chains stretch across many countries.
summary: About half of world trade runs through global supply chains, like the iPhone 3GS's. Globalization lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses piled up in particular places.

cards.headline: In March 2021, one stuck ship held up about $9 billion of trade a day.
cards.body: The Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal on March 23 and wasn't refloated until March 29. How could one ship matter so much? Because much of what you buy is pieced together across many countries.

cards.headline: Made in many places
cards.body: About half of global trade now happens inside global supply chains: networks that build products from parts and services sourced around the world. Take the iPhone 3GS. Its parts came from firms in Japan, South Korea, Germany and the US. Then it was all assembled in China.

cards.fact: Assembly in China added $6.50 to an iPhone 3GS that cost $178.96 to make.
cards.context: That's about 3.6% of the total, by economists Yuqing Xing and Neal Detert's 2010 count. Yet trade statistics recorded all $178.96 as a Chinese export. Remember Level 73's trade balance, exports minus imports? With supply chains, the country on the label isn't always where most of the value was made.

mascot.line: Keep this: the label names where it was finished, not where most of the value was made.

cards.headline: Two sides of the same story
cards.body: Supporters point to prices and growth: globalization lets countries specialize, which lowers prices, and more open economies helped once extremely poor countries grow and cut poverty. Critics point to who paid. Economists including David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson estimated that cheap Chinese imports cost the US roughly 2 million to 2.4 million jobs from 1999 to 2011, concentrated in places that stayed worse off for years. Meanwhile, consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods. Both are true at once.

cards.headline: Globalization
learned: About half of trade runs through global supply chains
An iPhone 3GS's parts came from four countries
Trade statistics can misplace where value is made
Lower prices and growth, but concentrated job losses

questions.prompt: Match each globalization example with its description.

pairs.right: About $9 billion of trade a day

questions.explanation: The iPhone 3GS was built from parts sourced worldwide and assembled in China. The stuck Ever Given held up about $9 billion of trade a day. Cheap Chinese imports cost the US roughly 2 million to 2.4 million jobs.

questions.prompt: Why do critics of globalization point to particular towns rather than the whole US?

options.label: Import-driven job losses were concentrated there
Those towns paid higher prices for goods
options.rationale: Consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods, those towns included.

options.label: Only those towns traded with any other countries
Those towns had no factories to begin with
options.rationale: The losses were in places that had factories and lost jobs.

questions.explanation: The China shock's job losses piled up in particular places, which stayed worse off, while consumers everywhere got slightly cheaper goods.

questions.prompt: GDP can be counted as value added at each stage of production. How much value did China's assembly add to an iPhone 3GS?

options.label: All $178.96
options.rationale: That's what trade statistics recorded, not the value China added.

options.label: About half the cost
options.rationale: Assembly was a small share, about 3.6%.

options.label: Nothing at all
options.rationale: Assembly did add value, just not much.

questions.explanation: Assembly added about $6.50 of the $178.96; counting value added shows most of it was made elsewhere.
